content:
Yesterday we saw that the Second Passover provision was given to two kinds of people; those who were ceremonially unclean, and those who were on a journey too far from home. We ended there, saying we would look more carefully at what these two groups mean for us. In Numbers 9, uncleanness could come in many ways; childbirth, skin disease, bodily discharge, contact with an unclean person or animal. But the men who came to Moses that day had become unclean specifically through touching a dead body. That is what the text focuses on. And so that is where we begin.

Under the Law of Moses, a person who had touched a dead body was shut out. They were defiled. They could not come near the altar, could not join the congregation at worship, could not take part in the Passover. There was no mercy clause built into that first Passover. The rule was clear; you are unclean, you cannot come. And if they tried to come anyway, the consequences were serious. The Law was holy, and it kept holy things holy by keeping defiled things away.

Now we need to ask the deeper question. In the picture Yahweh has built here, who do these unclean people represent? The answer is one we must sit with, because it covers the whole world. Paul says it in Romans 3:23 without any exception: all have sinned and come short of the glory of God. Not some people. Not people from certain backgrounds or certain nations. All. Every person born into this world from Adam onward carries the defilement of sin. We are, in the language of the Law, ceremonially unclean; dead in trespasses, shut out from God's presence, unable by our own effort to approach the altar. The unclean men in Numbers 9 who could not keep the Passover are a picture of the entire human family standing at a distance, defiled, excluded, with no way to come near on their own.

Now we come to the second group; those who were on a journey. These were not wicked people. They had not sinned deliberately. They were not avoiding the Passover. They simply found themselves far from the appointed place, on a road that had taken them away from home, and the distance made it impossible for them to be there on the fourteenth day of the first month. They wanted to come. They just could not get back in time.

And this, too, is a picture of the whole human family. Man was not always far from God. Adam was placed in Eden; God's garden, God's presence, the original home of mankind. But sin drove him out. And from that day to this, every person born into this world is born on a journey; far from the Father's house, far from the presence of God. The whole world is travelling through a wilderness, displaced, distant, longing for something they cannot name. Ecclesiastes 3:11 says that God has put eternity in the hearts of men. Every human carries a deep homesickness for something they have never seen in this life but somehow know they have lost. That is the traveller in Numbers 9. Far from the altar. Wanting to come home. Unable to get there by themselves.

So we have two pictures side by side; the unclean who are defiled and shut out, and the traveller who is distant and cannot find their way back. Together they cover everyone. And together they are the people for whom the Second Passover provision was made. Yahweh looked at the unclean and the far-away, and He said: there is still a way. Come one month later. The lamb will be ready. And this is where the picture opens up into something much larger than a rule in the wilderness.

In Numbers 9, the Second Passover was not a lesser version of the first.
The unclean man and the travelling man did not get a smaller sacrifice or a reduced memorial. They got the same lamb, the same blood, the same Passover; full provision, nothing taken away. Yahweh did not lower the standard for the defiled and the distant. He gave them the complete covenant, one month later, when they were able to come. This is the heart of the picture. God never gives His people a reduced version of His mercy.

Now we see what this was pointing toward all along. It is a picture of the Kingdom of Christ;, the great provision of God for all of humanity, not just for those who were clean and near during the first age. In the Kingdom, the unclean will be made clean. Zechariah 13:1 says: in that day there shall be a fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness. The travellers who have been far from home for their entire lives will finally come home. Micah 4:2 says: many nations shall come and say, come, let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh. The long journey will be over.

Christ himself made this clear. He said in John 6:51: the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world; not for the life of the church only, not for Israel only, but for the life of the world. Every person that was unclean, every person that was far away, every person that missed the first Passover under the old covenant, will be given this bread in the Kingdom age. John 6:37 says it without condition: whoever comes to me I will never cast out. No cleanness requirement. No distance too far. The Second Passover lamb is ready, and the provision is complete.

This is the God we serve. He did not write off the unclean. He did not abandon the traveller. He built the remedy into the Law itself, long before the Kingdom was proclaimed, as a quiet announcement that no one who truly hungers will be left without bread. The first Passover was for those who were clean and near. The second was for everyone else. And the true Second Passover; Christ, the Lamb of God - is the provision for the whole world now and in the age to come.

title: Prayer
text:
**Yahweh is gracious and full of compassion, slow to anger and great in mercy. Psalm 145:8**

O God, our Father,

We see ourselves in both groups today.

We were unclean; and we could not clean ourselves.

We were far from home; and we could not find the way back on our own.

And yet You did not close the door.

You built a second window into the very Law that shut us out,

and at the right time, You sent the true Passover Lamb for us.

We thank You that Your mercy is not just for those who had it together;

it is for the defiled, the wandering, the ones who missed every appointment.

And we hold onto the hope of the Kingdom, when the unclean world will be made clean,

and every traveller who has been far from home will finally come in.

We thank you in the name of Christ, Amen.
